metaTitle: Does Vinegar Kill Ants? It Won't Reach the Nest
metaDescription: Vinegar can wipe away an ant scent trail, but extension guides say the ants you see are a small part of the colony. See what vinegar does and what works.
h1: Does Vinegar Kill Ants? What It Does to Ants, Trails and Colonies
dek: What university extension guides say about vinegar and ants: it can clean up a scent trail for a while, it does not reach the queen, and bait is what ends the trail.
excerpt: Vinegar can wipe up an ant trail for a while, but it does not reach the queen or the nest. What extension guides say, when to skip it, and what ends the trail.

quickAnswer.lead: **Vinegar cleans up an ant trail; it does not kill the colony.** [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/got-ants-eliminate-them-with-ipm) lists a vinegar and water solution among the ways to wipe up ants' chemical trails, but the ants you see are a small portion of the colony, and no source shows vinegar reaching the nest. Bait that workers carry home is what ends the problem.
bullets: Penn State Extension lists a vinegar and water solution, or soapy water, for wiping up ant trails, and it gives no ratio.
No source reviewed measures how many ants vinegar kills on contact; the University of California says soap products such as window cleaners can kill ants on contact.
The ants on a counter are a small portion of the colony, and thousands more, including egg-laying queens, stay hidden in the nest, according to the University of Kentucky.
Ant bait can take 5 to 10 days to show fewer ants and may need several weeks or more to finish the job, according to the University of California.
Iowa State says not to use cleaning agents or insecticides around baits, so wipe away from the bait stations.

body.text: Does vinegar kill ants?

Not reliably, and it does not reach the colony. None of the extension and university guides reviewed for this page lists vinegar as an ant killer, and none measures how many ants a splash of it kills. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/got-ants-eliminate-them-with-ipm) mentions vinegar once, as a cleaning step: it lists a vinegar and water solution, or soapy water, for wiping up the chemical trails ants follow. Wiping a trail is cleanup, not treatment.

That gap in the evidence does not prove that vinegar sprayed on a few ants does nothing to them. It means no tested figure exists in these sources, so this page does not offer one. What the sources do establish is that killing the ants you can see is not the goal. The [University of Kentucky's ant control fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef619) calls spraying only the ants you see the mistake most people make, because those foragers are a small portion of the colony. Typically there are thousands more, including one or more egg-laying queens, hidden in a nest.

Products made to kill ants fall short when they are used the same way. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension](https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ants_household_B6183.pdf) says insecticides sprayed on ant trails kill only a few foraging workers and do not eliminate colonies. If an insecticide on a trail cannot end a colony, there is no reason to expect a kitchen liquid to. For how colonies work and which species you are likely dealing with, see [the complete guide to ants in US homes](/learn/ants).
What does vinegar do to an ant trail?

It can wipe away the scent trail the ants were following, and the two sources that say how long the relief lasts, Kentucky and the University of California, both call it temporary. Texas A&M says foraging workers of some species secrete chemical (pheromone) trails that lead other ants to food and water. [Colorado State University Extension](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/ants-in-the-home/) says workers lay these trails as they forage, and its advice once ants have been foraging in a home is to wash counters and floors with a household cleaner to eliminate the odor trails.

The [University of California Statewide IPM Program](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/ants/) (UC IPM) says soapy water removes the scent trail, especially when the cleaning is thorough at entry points, and that vacuuming or sponging a trail with soapy water may be as effective as an insecticide spray at temporarily removing foraging ants.

body.text: Soap or a general household cleaner is named in each of the four sources that describe wiping a trail (UC IPM, Penn State, Kentucky and Colorado State), and vinegar in only one. The supportable claim is that a vinegar and water wipe is an accepted way to clean a trail, not that it beats soap. Soap is the better-supported ingredient here: UC IPM says soap products such as window cleaners can kill ants on contact, and no source says the same of vinegar.

body.text: How do you use vinegar to clean up an ant trail?

Wipe the trail once, after you know what the ants are after, and treat it as the first step of a plan rather than the plan. Penn State lists the wipe among its non-chemical steps for ants indoors, and UC IPM's steps for an ant emergency start with removing the food source.

items: Find what the ants want and remove it. UC IPM puts this first, and Texas A&M adds cleaning up spilled food and drinks and storing food in tightly sealed containers.

Vacuum up the ants on the trail, then wipe it with a vinegar and water solution or with soapy water, taking extra care at the spot where the ants come in. Penn State gives no ratio, so the sources do not settle how much vinegar to use.

Seal the entry point. UC IPM says to locate entry points and then caulk the openings or plug them with petroleum jelly, and Penn State advises sealing cracks and crevices around windows, doors and pipes with caulk.
Fix the water. Texas A&M lists repairing dripping faucets and plumbing leaks, and UC IPM notes that leaky faucets attract thirsty ants.
If ants are back within days, put bait beside the trail and stop wiping that spot, for the reasons covered below.

body.text: Will vinegar kill the colony or the queen?

No. A wipe or a spray reaches only the ants that are out foraging, while the queens and the young stay hidden. [Iowa State University Extension](https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/ant-baits-small-household-ants) says sprays may affect only the small portion of the colony that is looking for food, and that queens and other colony members hidden in wall voids, behind cabinets or appliances, or in door and window frames are not affected. Texas A&M adds that most indoor nests cannot be seen because they sit in wall voids or under slabs.

Kentucky puts the goal in one line: eliminating queens and other colony members within nests is often the key to effective ant control. Queens lay the eggs, according to UC IPM, so a colony that keeps its queen keeps replacing the workers you wipe up. [How long worker ants and queens live, by species](/blog/how-long-do-ants-live) shows how long that can go on.
What about pouring vinegar on an ant hill?

The sources that mention pouring liquid on a nest name hot soapy water and boiling water, not vinegar. Penn State says ant nests can be destroyed or discouraged by digging them up or soaking them with hot, soapy water. Colorado State says boiling water can kill small colonies that do not extend deeply, but large, deep or hard-to-reach colonies cannot be managed that way, and the hazards of handling it generally exceed those of using ant insecticides, with less chance of success.

No source reviewed here tests vinegar on a nest. A nest that runs deep or sits inside a wall is out of reach of anything poured on the surface, which is the limit Colorado State describes for boiling water. Mounds of stinging red imported fire ants are a separate case, covered in [how to tell fire ants from the red look-alikes](/blog/red-ants).
Does vinegar keep ants away?

No source reviewed for this page shows that it does. Kentucky and UC IPM call the effect of wiping a trail temporary, and no source gives a duration. UC IPM pairs the wipe with removing the food source and caulking entry points. Texas A&M says ants enter a home in search of food, water or a good nesting site, so a wipe that leaves all three in place gives the ants no reason to stay away.

Repellents do exist, and the sources keep them apart from cleaners. Texas A&M says some contact insecticides repel ants, naming pyrethroids such as permethrin and bifenthrin. It says repellents should not be used while baits are set out, though they can be used after a baiting program, or sprayed around cracks and openings as a barrier. Vinegar appears in none of those lists, and any such product must be used as its label directs.
Can vinegar make an ant problem worse?
It can if it replaces the step that works. The sources describe three ways a spray or a cleanup can backfire, and none of them tested vinegar, so read these as cautions rather than findings about it.

items: **Splitting the colony.** Texas A&M says insecticides sprayed on ant trails can sometimes make the problem worse by causing a colony to split into two or more separate colonies. Colorado State reports that pharaoh ants in particular may split colonies and scatter in response to disturbances, including the use of some insecticides. Both statements concern insecticides, and neither mentions vinegar.

**Keeping ants off the bait.** Iowa State says not to use cleaning agents or insecticides around baits, because sprays and cleansers may deter ants from approaching and eating the bait. Vinegar is used as a cleaner, so the caution reasonably applies to it.
**Treating a temporary fix as the cure.** Kentucky says wiping away odor trails gives temporary relief. A wipe leaves the nest, and the queens in it, untouched.

body.text: Can you use vinegar and ant bait together?

Yes, as long as the vinegar stays away from the bait and from the trail the ants use to reach it. The sources lean slightly different ways. UC IPM says to keep cleaning up trails while baits work, and not to use insecticide sprays while baiting. Kentucky says not to disturb foraging trails if you are using a bait. Iowa State says to keep counters and floors clean by sweeping and washing, but not to use cleaning agents or insecticides around the baits, and adds that bait works only if ants take it back to the colony, so you have to tolerate the extra activity while it does.
One reading that fits all three: wipe stray trails away from the bait stations, and leave the bait and the ants feeding at it alone.

body.title: Leave the ants at the bait alone
body.text: Kentucky says the number of ants around a bait usually rises at first, that this shows they are feeding and carrying the bait back to the nest, and that you should not spray them. Activity usually subsides in a few days as the colony shrinks.
What actually ends an ant trail?

A slow-acting bait that workers carry back to the nest, combined with removing the food and water that drew the ants and sealing the way in. UC IPM calls baits a key tool for managing ants and the only type of insecticide recommended in most situations, and its emergency steps say indoor sprays are not usually necessary. Penn State advises against sprays, bombs, foggers and liquid concentrates indoors, because they can irritate lungs, leave residues on indoor surfaces or be touched or swallowed by children, and recommends enclosed, tamper-resistant baits instead.

Bait works because of how ants share food. Iowa State says foraging workers carry it to the nest and feed it to the queen or queens and other colony members, so the entire colony can be destroyed. Texas A&M describes effective indoor bait ingredients as slow-acting, such as fipronil, hydramethylnon, boric acid and borax, and warns against confusing baits with bait traps that kill only foraging workers and not the ants in the nest. It also notes that some ant species feed mostly on sugar while others prefer oils or proteins, which is why [what ants eat and how that decides which bait they take](/blog/what-do-ants-eat) matters. Follow the product label for placement, amounts and safety.

body.text: Plan for weeks, not days. For the full indoor routine, see [the step-by-step plan for finding the entry point and baiting the colony](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-house). For food-prep areas, [where bait goes in a kitchen and what to keep it away from](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-kitchen) covers placement. If the ants are small and head for sweets, [which of the sweet-loving species you have](/blog/sugar-ants) helps you choose a bait.

Some people would rather mix their own, and [borax and boric acid as ant bait](/blog/borax-for-ants) explains how that works and where it fails. To compare ready-made options, [a comparison of ant killers that reach the colony](/blog/best-ant-killer) and [how bait stations differ from glue traps](/blog/best-ant-traps-canada) go through them. Vinegar is one of several home fixes people try first, and [when do-it-yourself pest control is worth doing and when to hire a professional](/blog/diy-pest-control) sets out where the line sits. Texas A&M's advice is that if you are not successful, you should call a commercial pest control operator.

faqs.question: Can I pour vinegar on an ant hill?
faqs.answer: No source reviewed for this page tests it. The extension guides that mention liquid on a nest name hot, soapy water for destroying or discouraging nests, according to Penn State, and boiling water for small, shallow colonies, according to Colorado State, which says large or deep colonies cannot be managed that way. A nest that runs deep is out of reach of a cup of anything. Digging out the nest, or baiting the colony, are the methods the sources describe.

faqs.question: Does white vinegar work better than apple cider vinegar on ants?
faqs.answer: The sources reviewed for this page do not compare types or strengths of vinegar. Penn State names only a vinegar and water solution for wiping up ants' chemical trails and gives no ratio or type. A claim that one kind kills more ants, or keeps them away longer, is not backed by the university and extension guides reviewed here. What they do support is the larger plan: remove the food and water, seal entry points and bait the colony.

faqs.question: Should I add dish soap to vinegar to kill ants?
faqs.answer: The sources do not test that mix. What they support is soap on its own. The University of California says soapy water removes an ant's scent trail and that soap products such as window cleaners can kill ants on contact without leaving a lasting toxic residue, and Penn State lists soapy water next to the vinegar solution. Soap is therefore the better-supported ingredient, but neither source claims either liquid reaches the nest.

faqs.question: How long will ants stay away after I wipe the trail with vinegar?
faqs.answer: No source gives a time. The University of Kentucky calls wiping away odor trails temporary relief, and the University of California describes soapy water as temporarily removing foraging ants. How long the relief lasts depends on whether the ants still have a reason to come back, such as food within reach, water and an open way in. The University of California lists removing the food source and caulking entry points in its emergency steps alongside the wipe.

faqs.question: What should I do if ants keep coming back after I use vinegar?
faqs.answer: Find where they enter and what they want, then switch to bait. The University of California suggests putting out bait stations or applying gel bait at entry points once the food source is removed and openings are sealed, and it says it can take 5 to 10 days to see fewer ants. Leave the bait and the trail to it alone while it works. Texas A&M says that if you are not successful, you should call a commercial pest control operator.
